title: Experiment Tracking and Reproducibility
definition: Systematic logging of hyperparameters, metrics, code versions, data versions, and artifacts for every training run. Tools: W&B (Weights & Biases), MLflow, TensorBoard. Reproducibility requires: fixed seeds, deterministic ops, versioned data, containerized environments. Formally, a reproducible experiment is a tuple $(\mathcal{D}, \theta, f, \text{env})$ — dataset, hyperparameters, code, environment — from which identical results can be regenerated.
intuition: Like a lab notebook for ML experiments. When your colleague asks 'what was the learning rate for the run that got 90% success?' you need an instant answer, not a folder of untitled scripts. Good tracking means any result can be reproduced by anyone on the team at any time.
practical_example: W&B setup for RL training: log every 1000 steps — reward $R_t$, episode length $T$, loss $\mathcal{L}$, entropy $H(\pi)$, learning rate $\alpha$. Log hyperparameters as config. Save model checkpoints as artifacts with data version tags. Custom W&B panels for comparing runs across hyperparameter sweeps. Use sweep agents for automated hyperparameter search (Bayesian optimization over $\alpha \in [10^{-5}, 10^{-3}]$, batch size $\in \{32, 64, 128, 256\}$).
failure_mode: Results not reproducible: 'worked on my machine' syndrome. Random seeds not fixed, GPU non-determinism, data pipeline changed between runs, library version drift. Symptoms: best result can't be recreated. Fix: log everything (code hash, pip freeze, data hash), use containers (Docker), set CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG for GPU determinism.
interview_answer: Experiment tracking is non-negotiable for professional ML work. My setup: W&B for metrics/hyperparams/artifacts, git for code, DVC for data versioning, Docker for environment reproducibility. Key principles: (1) every run must be reproducible from its logged config, (2) compare runs on equal footing (same eval protocol), (3) track compute cost alongside performance. In industry, the ability to trace any deployed model back to its exact training configuration is a hard requirement for debugging production issues.

title: Evaluation Methodology for Robot Learning
definition: Rigorous assessment of robot policy performance. Primary metric: success rate $\hat{p} = \frac{\text{successes}}{N_{\text{trials}}}$ with Wilson confidence interval: $$\hat{p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{N_{\text{trials}}}}$$ Includes: failure mode analysis, sim-to-real transfer gap $\Delta = p_{\text{sim}} - p_{\text{real}}$, generalization tests (novel objects, positions), robustness tests (perturbations), and statistical significance across seeds ($n \geq 3$).
intuition: A 90% success rate in the lab means nothing if you only tested on 10 trials with the same object in the same position. Proper evaluation means: 100+ trials, varied conditions, reporting confidence intervals, and categorizing failure modes. It's the difference between 'it works' and 'it works and I know when it will fail.'
practical_example: Manipulation policy evaluation: 100 trials across 5 object categories $\times$ 4 initial positions = 2000 total trials. Report: overall success rate ($85\% \pm 3\%$), per-category breakdown, failure mode taxonomy (grasp slip: 40% of failures, perception error: 30%, planning failure: 30%). Include sim and real results separately. Compute $p$-value via McNemar's test when comparing two policies on paired trials.
failure_mode: Cherry-picked results: only reporting best seed, testing only on easy configurations, not controlling for environmental variation. Also: sim evaluation doesn't predict real performance — policies that reach 99% in sim may drop to 60% in real ($\Delta_{\text{sim2real}} = 39\%$). Fix: always report real-robot results, use sufficient trial counts ($N \geq 50$), report standard deviation across seeds, test on held-out configurations.
interview_answer: Rigorous evaluation is what separates research demos from deployable systems. My evaluation protocol: (1) define success criteria precisely (binary success, not continuous metrics), (2) test across varied conditions (objects, positions, lighting), (3) report mean $\pm$ std across $\geq 3$ seeds and $\geq 50$ trials, (4) categorize every failure. In industry, I also add: edge case discovery (adversarial testing), long-horizon reliability (1000+ sequential executions), and degradation testing (what breaks first as conditions change). The most important metric is rarely the one in the paper — it's the failure mode distribution.

title: Deployment Thinking for Robot Systems
definition: Designing robot learning systems with deployment constraints in mind from day one: inference latency $t_{\text{infer}} < t_{\text{budget}}$, compute budget (FLOPS, memory), failure recovery, monitoring, and graceful degradation. The gap between a research demo and a production robot is mostly systems engineering. Key metrics: latency $p_{99}$, throughput, mean time between failures (MTBF), mean time to recovery (MTTR).
intuition: A research demo runs on an A100 with a human ready to hit the e-stop. A deployed system runs on an edge GPU 24/7 with no human in the loop. Deployment thinking means asking: 'What happens when the model outputs garbage? What if inference takes 200ms instead of 50ms? What if the camera gets occluded?'
practical_example: Deploying a pick-and-place policy: model distillation from a 300M parameter diffusion model to a 10M student model for edge inference. Add a confidence threshold — if the policy's predicted uncertainty $\hat{\sigma}$ exceeds a bound $\sigma_{\max}$, stop and request human intervention. Monitor: inference latency $p_{99}$, prediction confidence $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\sigma}]$, success rate rolling window (last 100 picks), camera health check (frame rate, exposure).
failure_mode: Silent failure: the system continues operating but performance degrades without alerting anyone. Example: camera calibration drifts over weeks, success rate slowly drops from 95% to 70%. Nobody notices until production quality complaints. Fix: continuous monitoring dashboards, automated performance regression alerts (trigger when success rate drops $> 5\%$ from baseline), periodic recalibration schedules.
interview_answer: Deployment is where most robot learning projects fail — not because the model is bad, but because the systems around it aren't robust. Key principles: (1) latency budget — know your control loop timing and design inference to fit ($t_{\text{infer}} < t_{\text{budget}}$), (2) failure detection — the system must know when it's failing (confidence estimation, anomaly detection), (3) graceful degradation — when confidence is low, fall back to safer behavior or stop, (4) monitoring — dashboards for success rate, latency, confidence distribution in production, (5) update pipeline — ability to retrain and redeploy without downtime. The question I always ask: 'What happens at 3 AM when nobody is watching?'

title: Inference Latency Optimization for Robot Control
definition: Reducing the time from observation to action output to meet real-time control requirements. Techniques: model distillation ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}} = \text{KL}(p_{\text{teacher}} \| p_{\text{student}})$), quantization (FP32 $\rightarrow$ FP16/INT8), TensorRT compilation, batched inference, async perception-control pipelines, model pruning (structured/unstructured). Target latencies: $< 50\,\text{ms}$ for manipulation, $< 10\,\text{ms}$ for reactive control, $< 1\,\text{ms}$ for joint-level servo.
intuition: A robot reaching for a moving object can't wait 500ms for a diffusion model to generate an action. Latency directly limits control bandwidth — at 100ms latency, you can only correct 10 times per second. Every millisecond matters for reactive, contact-rich tasks.
practical_example: Optimizing a diffusion policy: original (100 denoising steps, FP32) $\rightarrow$ 1.5s per action. Step 1: DDIM ($T=10$ steps) $\rightarrow$ 150ms. Step 2: FP16 inference $\rightarrow$ 100ms. Step 3: TensorRT compilation $\rightarrow$ 60ms. Step 4: async pipeline (predict next chunk while executing current) $\rightarrow$ effective 30ms latency. Total: $50\times$ speedup.
failure_mode: Optimized model has different behavior: quantization changes numerical outputs enough to affect policy behavior. Symptoms: policy works in FP32 but fails in FP16/INT8 — subtle action differences compound over a trajectory. Fix: calibrate quantization on representative data, validate post-optimization on full evaluation suite, use mixed-precision (sensitive layers in FP32).
interview_answer: Latency optimization is critical for deploying learned robot policies. My optimization stack: (1) algorithmic — reduce denoising steps with DDIM/consistency models, (2) numerical — FP16 inference, mixed precision where needed, (3) compilation — TensorRT/ONNX for GPU, TFLite for edge, (4) architectural — async pipelines so inference runs in parallel with execution. Key insight: it's often better to use a smaller, faster model with slightly lower accuracy than a large slow one — the control bandwidth improvement more than compensates. Target latencies: $< 50\,\text{ms}$ for pick-and-place, $< 10\,\text{ms}$ for contact-rich tasks, $< 1\,\text{ms}$ for joint-level reactive control.

title: Dataset Curation for Robot Learning
definition: The systematic process of collecting, filtering, balancing, and versioning demonstration datasets for training robot policies. Quality matters more than quantity: a policy trained on $N$ high-quality demonstrations often outperforms one trained on $10N$ noisy ones. Key considerations: state-action coverage $\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{D}) = \text{vol}(\text{support}(\mathcal{D}))$ over the relevant task manifold, data balance across modes/conditions, outlier removal, and consistent labeling. For multi-task datasets, maintain per-task statistics and ensure no task is severely underrepresented ($N_{\text{task}_i} \geq N_{\min}$ for all $i$).
intuition: Garbage in, garbage out — but for robots, this is even more critical because bad demonstrations teach bad physical habits. A dataset with 1000 demos where the robot always approaches from the right will produce a policy that can't handle left-side approaches. Curation means ensuring your training data covers the situations the robot will actually encounter, with consistent quality throughout.
practical_example: Curating a bimanual manipulation dataset: (1) Collect 500 teleoperated demonstrations across 10 tasks. (2) Automated filtering: discard episodes where task success is ambiguous, joint velocity exceeds safety limits ($\|\dot{q}\| > \dot{q}_{\max}$), or gripper force is anomalous. (3) Balance check: ensure each task has $\geq 40$ demos, each object orientation bin has $\geq 10$ demos. (4) Quality audit: human reviews a random 10% sample for labeling accuracy. (5) Augmentation: for underrepresented regions, collect targeted demonstrations. (6) Version with DVC: tag as `v1.2`, log statistics (per-task counts, action distribution plots, state-space coverage heatmaps). Result: 420 clean demos that train a better policy than the original 500.
failure_mode: Distribution mismatch: training data collected in one setting (single table, good lighting) but deployed in another (different table height, variable lighting). Covariate shift causes policy failure on out-of-distribution observations. Also: demonstrator inconsistency — multiple operators with different styles create conflicting multi-modal data that confuses unimodal policies. Symptoms: policy works in the training environment but fails in deployment; policy exhibits hesitant or averaged behavior. Fix: collect data across deployment conditions, standardize operator instructions, use multi-modal policy architectures (diffusion) for multi-operator data, track and visualize data distribution coverage.
interview_answer: Dataset curation is arguably the highest-leverage activity in robot learning — more impactful than architecture search or hyperparameter tuning. My curation pipeline: (1) define coverage requirements upfront (task variations, object diversity, approach directions), (2) collect with quality checks in the loop (real-time visualization, automated anomaly detection), (3) post-collection filtering (success verification, kinematic feasibility, statistical outlier removal), (4) balance analysis and targeted augmentation for underrepresented regions, (5) version everything with DVC. Key insight: invest time in understanding your data distribution before training. I always plot action distributions, state-space coverage, and per-task statistics. A common mistake: collecting 1000 demos of the easy case and 10 of the hard case — the policy will only learn the easy case.

title: Runtime Safety Monitoring for Robot Systems
definition: Continuous verification during robot execution that safety constraints are satisfied. Formalized as monitoring a set of safety predicates $\{\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_M\}$ at each control step, where violation of any predicate triggers a safety response. Common constraints: workspace bounds $\mathbf{p}_{\text{ee}} \in \mathcal{W}_{\text{safe}}$, velocity limits $\|\dot{\mathbf{q}}\| \leq \dot{q}_{\max}$, force/torque limits $\|\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{ext}}\| \leq \tau_{\max}$, collision avoidance $d(\text{robot}, \text{obstacle}) \geq d_{\min}$, and self-collision checking. Multi-layered: from low-level hardware e-stops to high-level learned anomaly detection.
intuition: A self-driving car has multiple safety systems: lane departure warning, automatic braking, airbags. Robot systems need the same layered approach. The learned policy is like the driver — usually good, but can make mistakes. Safety monitoring is the set of guardrails that prevent those mistakes from causing damage: hard limits the policy can never exceed, soft limits that trigger caution, and anomaly detection that flags when something unexpected is happening.
practical_example: Safety stack for a collaborative robot manipulation system: Layer 1 (hardware, $< 1\,\text{ms}$): joint torque limits, e-stop circuit. Layer 2 (real-time controller, $< 5\,\text{ms}$): workspace bounds check $\mathbf{p}_{\text{ee}} \in \mathcal{W}$, velocity scaling near limits ($v_{\text{scale}} = \min(1, d_{\text{boundary}} / d_{\text{margin}})$), collision checking against known geometry. Layer 3 (policy level, $< 50\,\text{ms}$): action clipping to kinematically feasible set, confidence-based speed scaling ($v \propto \text{confidence}$). Layer 4 (high-level, $< 1\,\text{s}$): learned anomaly detector (autoencoder on observation history, trigger when reconstruction error $\|o - \hat{o}\| > \epsilon_{\text{anomaly}}$), task progress monitoring (detect if stuck or regressing). Each layer has a defined response: Layer 1 = hard stop, Layer 2 = velocity reduction + alert, Layer 3 = conservative fallback behavior, Layer 4 = pause and request human review.
failure_mode: Safety monitor is too conservative: overly tight bounds cause frequent unnecessary stops, reducing throughput and annoying operators. Safety monitor is too permissive: bounds set during benign testing miss edge cases in deployment (e.g., a new obstacle not in the collision model). Latent failure: safety monitor itself fails silently (sensor providing safety data dies). Symptoms: either constant false alarms or a real safety incident that monitoring should have caught. Fix: tune safety bounds with deployment data, use redundant sensing for critical monitors, monitor the monitors (watchdog timers, heartbeat checks), conduct regular safety audits with adversarial testing.
interview_answer: Runtime safety monitoring is non-negotiable for deployed robot systems. I design safety as a layered architecture: hardware limits (always-on, cannot be overridden by software), real-time geometric checks (workspace bounds, collision avoidance at $> 100\,\text{Hz}$), policy-level guards (action feasibility, confidence thresholds), and high-level anomaly detection (learned models that flag out-of-distribution situations). Key design principles: (1) defense in depth — every layer is independent, (2) fail-safe defaults — unknown = stop, (3) monitor the monitors — watchdogs and redundancy, (4) graceful degradation — reduce speed before stopping entirely. The hardest part: tuning thresholds that are safe without being so conservative they prevent useful work. I always start conservative and relax based on operational data, never the other way around.
